_README: Researched prose for individual spots, keyed by spot slug. This is the depth layer that the Supabase `spots` row cannot carry: the row holds structured fields (species, gear, best_times, access), and rendering those as bulleted lists is what produced a 209-word templated page and two AdSense low-value-content rejections. Prose lives here rather than in Supabase for the same reason country-guides.json does — it is authored and reviewed in git, and it sidesteps the migration-before-build ordering hazard entirely. Unlike country-guides.json, sections are an ARRAY with per-spot headings rather than fixed keys: every country genuinely has licensing/seasons/water, but a lodge-only Patagonian lake and an urban harbour share no structure, and 49 pages carrying identical headings would be a longer template rather than an escape from one. `sources` IS rendered — visible citation is the point. `sourcing` and `sourceNotes` are never rendered; they record what was verified and, more usefully, what was deliberately left out for lack of an official page. Read sourceNotes before adding to a spot. Validate with `node scripts/check-spot-guides.mjs` before committing. Content rules 1 and 3 apply in full: no claim without a traceable official source, and no bag or size numbers even when the official source prints them.

sections.heading: Who controls the fishing
sections.body: There is no general public right to fish for salmon in Scotland, and on the Spey that abstract point takes a very concrete form: the river is divided into privately managed beats, and the only lawful way onto one is a permit from the estate or association that holds it. Above the beats sits the Spey Fishery Board, a statutory body drawing its powers from the Salmon and Freshwater Fisheries (Consolidation) (Scotland) Act 2003 — the modern successor to the Victorian salmon fisheries legislation that created district boards in the first place. A district salmon fishery board is not a club or a lobby group. It is the legal management authority for its catchment, and the Spey Board's remit runs to the conservation and protection of Atlantic salmon and sea trout across the whole river. A visiting angler therefore deals with two layers: the beat, which sells the day and usually provides the ghillie, and the Board, whose rules apply whichever beat you happen to be standing on.

sections.heading: What the conservation designation says about the water
sections.body: The Spey is a Special Area of Conservation and a Site of Special Scientific Interest, and the official citation describes the water more precisely than most angling write-ups manage. JNCC lists four qualifying species: Atlantic salmon, freshwater pearl mussel, sea lamprey and otter. On salmon it records that the Spey "supports one of the largest Atlantic salmon populations in Scotland", with good-quality nursery habitat, water that is "largely unpolluted" and a channel "relatively free from flow modifications" — the technical way of saying the river still behaves like a river, with clean gravels and an unobstructed migration route to the sea. The middle and lower reaches hold what JNCC calls "a pearl mussel population of great international significance", and those same reaches carry sea lamprey larvae at the northern edge of the species' British range. The designated site covers 5,759 hectares.

sections.heading: The season, Sundays and the release policy
sections.body: Two separate regimes govern when you may fish. The annual close time is set district by district in Scottish regulations rather than nationally, so the Spey's opening and closing dates are a matter of statutory instrument and are the thing to confirm before you book anything. Sundays are simpler and absolute: section 13 of the 2003 Act states that "no person shall fish for or take salmon during Sunday", and the weekly close time it establishes runs from six on Friday evening to six the following Monday morning, with rod and line permitted on the Friday, Saturday and Monday inside that window. Release policy is layered in the same way. Scottish legislation requires that every salmon caught before 1 April is returned alive; the Board's own conservation policy, which has run since 2003, extends mandatory release to the end of May, asks that hen fish are returned throughout the season, and sets size thresholds above and below which sea trout must go back. The Board reports that release rates now run at around 98 per cent. Confirm the current policy with the Board before travelling — the detail is revised between seasons.

sections.heading: The dietary advice, and the line at the Harbour Bridge
sections.body: Sydney Harbour is one of the great urban fisheries and it carries a health advisory that most guides to it never mention. NSW Government dietary advice is that no fish or crustaceans caught west of the Sydney Harbour Bridge should be eaten at all, and that catches taken east of the bridge should be limited to 150 grams per month. The bridge is not a convenient landmark here — it is the actual line the advice draws. The cause is dioxin, traced to contaminated sediments near Homebush Bay, where a chemical works operated for four decades from the 1940s; the compounds are persistent, they sit in the sediment rather than the water column, and they accumulate up the food chain, which is why the advice tightens the further west you fish. Commercial fishing and prawn trawling have been banned harbour-wide since 2006 as a result. Multilingual warning signs are posted around the foreshore, which is a fair indication of how seriously the advice is meant. None of this is a reason not to fish the harbour. It is a reason to know, before you keep anything, which side of the bridge you were standing on.

sections.heading: Recreational fishing continues — with conditions
sections.body: The 2006 ban applies to commercial operators. Recreational fishing was not banned and remains open across the harbour, and catch-and-release is entirely unaffected by the dietary advice, which concerns eating fish rather than catching them. For a kingfish fishery this matters less than it would elsewhere: much of the sport here is releasing fish anyway. Anyone aged eighteen or over must hold a current NSW Recreational Fishing Fee receipt and carry it while fishing, and the fee applies in saltwater as well as fresh. Beyond that, the harbour is a working port and a heavily regulated waterway — aquatic reserves, intertidal protected areas and other location closures each cover parts of it, and they are not uniform. NSW publishes the closures for Port Jackson by location rather than as a single harbour-wide rule, so the sensible order is to check the closure map for the specific stretch you intend to fish before you go, rather than assume the harbour is one jurisdiction. Public ramps are mapped by Transport for NSW; trailer parking at the popular inner-harbour ramps is limited, particularly at weekends.

sections.heading: The river the management area was built around
sections.body: The Kenai River is one of very few Alaskan waterways managed under a dedicated special management area, and the designation is not cosmetic. The Kenai River Special Management Area was established by the Alaska Department of Natural Resources to govern both the riparian habitat and the human access along a corridor of the river that runs through some of the most heavily fished water in the state. The management plan is explicit that its purpose is to protect the river's anadromous fish habitat while providing recreational access, and the infrastructure on the ground reflects that compromise: at Soldotna, Centennial Park alone carries twenty-five sets of access stairs to the bank, two elevated platforms reaching eighty-five feet, and roughly ten boardwalk landings, several of them wheelchair accessible. The stairs and boardwalks are not a convenience — they are the access policy made physical. The management area requires anglers to stay on the constructed walkways, which keeps foot traffic off the spawning gravels and the riparian vegetation that shades the redds. The visitor centre at Soldotna is the practical starting point for understanding which rules apply to which section of river, because the regulations are not uniform along the corridor.

sections.heading: Emergency orders are the rule, not the exception
sections.body: The Kenai is managed in real time, and the mechanism for that is the emergency order. Alaska Department of Fish and Game issues emergency orders throughout the season to adjust king salmon retention, bait restrictions and gear limits on specific river sections, sometimes with only days of notice. The reason is that king salmon runs vary enormously between years, and the department's mandate is to respond to the run strength rather to a fixed regulation printed months earlier. The practical consequence for a visiting angler is that the regulations in force on the day you arrive may differ materially from what the guidebooks printed last winter. ADF&G publishes the current emergency orders on its Southcentral region page and updates them as the season develops. King salmon restrictions are the most visible: in years when the run is weak, the river may be closed to king salmon retention entirely, with mandatory release on all kings regardless of section. In stronger years, limited retention may be permitted in specific sections. The sockeye runs, which are the numerical backbone of the fishery, are managed on a two-run cycle: the first run arrives in June and the second, larger run peaks from mid-July through August. Rainbow trout fishing improves through September and October, when the spawning sockeye draw predators into the shallows.

sections.heading: The licence and the stamp
sections.body: An Alaska sport fishing licence is required, and anyone retaining king salmon must also hold a king salmon stamp, which is a separate validation added to the licence. The stamp requirement is specific to kings and does not apply to sockeye, coho or other species. The licence itself is available online through ADF&G or from licensed vendors throughout the Kenai Peninsula. Residents and non-residents have different fee structures, and the non-resident licence is the one most visitors will need. Beyond the licence, the Kenai has specific bait and gear restrictions that vary by section and season. The Upper Kenai, above Skilak Lake, has historically carried bait restrictions during parts of the salmon season, and emergency orders can extend or modify those restrictions in-year. The section-by-section approach means that a reach open to bait one week may be closed the next, which is why checking the current emergency orders before each trip is not optional — it is the only way to know what is actually in force.

sections.heading: The tag, not the harvest
sections.body: Florida's tarpon fishery operates on a principle that most harvest fisheries do not: the default is release, and keeping a tarpon requires a specific harvest tag that very few anglers hold. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission requires that any angler who has not been issued a tarpon harvest tag must release the fish alive, and the tag itself is limited — FWC allocates a fixed number per year, they are issued by lottery, and the overwhelming majority of tarpon caught in the Keys are released under the tagless default. The regulation exists because tarpon are slow-growing and late-maturing, and the stock cannot sustain harvest at the level of angling pressure the Keys receive. Beyond the tag rule, anyone aged sixteen or over who is not a Florida resident must hold a valid saltwater fishing licence, and FWC requires that the licence be carried while fishing. The licence is available online and the fee structure differs for residents and non-residents. The rules for bonefish and permit follow the same framework: both are catch-and-release by default, with no open season and no harvest permitted without a specific permit. The Keys are not unusual in this — the entire South Florida zone operates under the same catch-and-release mandate for these species — but the concentration of guides and charter operators in Islamorada means the release culture is more visible here than almost anywhere else.

sections.heading: Founders Park and the boundaries visitors miss
sections.body: The Village of Islamorada signs Founders Park as no-fishing, and the restriction is easy to miss because the park is one of the most visible landmarks on the Overseas Highway through the village. The prohibition covers the park grounds and the adjacent shoreline, and it applies to all fishing — not just a particular method or season. The Village's public boat ramp, at the Plantation Yacht Harbor Marina, is the correct launch point for anglers heading onto the flats, and it is a separate facility from Founders Park. The ramp is staffed during marina hours and carries a launch fee for non-residents; Village residents launch free on production of valid ID. The fee is charged in each direction, so a round trip is two charges. The ramp is the only public launch in the village itself, and trailer parking is dedicated but limited at peak times. Beyond the village, the flats fishing extends across both the Atlantic and Gulf sides of the Keys chain, and the management jurisdiction shifts between FWC's Atlantic and Gulf zones, which carry different species rules. The boundary between zones runs through the middle of Islamorada, which means that the same species may be subject to different regulations on the ocean side versus the bay side of the same island.

sections.heading: Tides, not calendars
sections.body: The tarpon migration through the middle Keys peaks from April through July, but the daily fishing is governed more by tide than by month. Moving tides — the two- to three-hour windows around slack water turning to ebb or flood — are when tarpon are most active on the flats, because the tidal movement pushes baitfish through the channels and the predators follow. Dawn and dusk overlaps with the moving tide are the most productive windows, and guides plan their days around the tide tables rather than the calendar. Outside the peak migration, tarpon are present year-round in smaller numbers, and the backcountry channels hold fish through the winter months when the flats are quieter. The bonefish and permit fishery follows a similar tidal pattern but without the strong seasonal migration: these species are resident on the flats and their behaviour is driven by tide height, water clarity and wind more than by calendar date. The practical implication is that a trip planned around the wrong tide window will find empty flats even in the peak month, while a trip on a modest day with the right tide can produce well. FWC does not set tidal restrictions — these are biological patterns — but the commission does set the framework within which guides operate, and the commercial guide licensing requirement means that anyone charging for flats fishing in the Keys must hold a valid FWC saltwater products licence.

sections.heading: Beats, not banks — how access actually works
sections.body: The Tweed is Scotland's most productive Atlantic salmon river by some measures, and the access system that governs it is the same one that governs every salmon river north of the border: the river is divided into beats, and each beat is managed by the estate or association that holds the fishing rights. There is no rod licence in Scotland. There is no Environment Agency equivalent that issues a blanket permission. The legal requirement is that you hold the permission of the beat owner, and on the Tweed that permission is sold as a day ticket, a season ticket or a package with guide and boat, depending on the beat. Popular autumn beats are booked well in advance, and the booking window for the best beats on the upper river routinely opens months before the season starts. The Tweed Foundation, which is the district salmon fishery board for the catchment, maintains a listing of available beats and the contacts for each one. A beat on the Tweed is not a single bank — it is a defined stretch of river, often both banks, and the fishing rights include the bed and the right to fish it. The estate typically provides a ghillie who knows the beat, reads the water and puts visiting anglers on fish. The ghillie is not a luxury — on a river this size and this varied, local knowledge of where the fish are holding is the difference between a productive day and a long walk.

sections.heading: The cross-border complication
sections.body: The Tweed forms the border between Scotland and England for much of its lower course, and the jurisdictional question is not academic: Scottish and English fisheries law diverged when Scotland kept its district board system and England moved to the Environment Agency rod licence model. On the Scottish side of the river, the Tweed Foundation's rules apply. On the English side, the Environment Agency licence is required in addition to the beat permission. The river itself does not mark the boundary clearly in every reach — the border follows the thread of the channel in some sections and the high-water mark in others, and the beat boundaries do not always correspond to the jurisdictional line. The practical consequence is that an angler fishing a beat that straddles the border may need both permissions, and the beat owner or ghillie is the person to clarify which side of the line a particular pool sits on. The Tweed Foundation's jurisdiction runs to the catchment as a whole, and its conservation rules apply to the river regardless of which bank you are standing on, but the licensing requirement is jurisdiction-specific.

sections.heading: The autumn run, the spring fish and the Sunday prohibition
sections.body: The Tweed's salmon run peaks in autumn, with the best fishing from September through November when the river is in colour and the fish are pushing upstream into the tributaries. Spring fish arrive from February through April, and the spring fishing is a different proposition: lower water, fewer fish and a mandatory release policy that has been in place on the Tweed for several years as a conservation measure. The Tweed Foundation's conservation policy requires that all spring salmon are returned alive, and the policy extends to hen fish throughout the season in most years. The Foundation reports that the Tweed's salmon returns have declined in line with the North Atlantic trend, and the release policy is the response to that decline. The Sunday prohibition is separate from the conservation policy and older: section 13 of the Salmon and Freshwater Fisheries (Consolidation) (Scotland) Act 2003 states that no person shall fish for or take salmon during Sunday, and the weekly close time runs from Friday evening through Monday morning. This applies across Scotland, not just the Tweed, and there are no exceptions. The autumn run is the most reliable window for visiting anglers, but the river fishes throughout the season and the tributaries — the Teviot, the Ettrick, the Gala Water — each have their own character and their own beats.

sections.heading: The fishery that needs no licence
sections.body: Sea angling in Norway is free. There is no rod licence, no permit fee and no registration requirement for recreational fishing from the shore or from a boat in saltwater, and this applies to Norwegian residents and visiting anglers alike. The Directorate of Fisheries sets the rules, but the rules are permissive by default: handheld tackle — rod and handline — is open to everyone, and the only universal restrictions are that you must stay more than 100 metres from the nearest fish farm and that you may not sell what you catch. The no-sale rule is absolute for recreational anglers and is enforced under the same regulations that keep the fishery open. The 100-metre fish farm buffer is a more recent addition, introduced after interactions between anglers and aquaculture operations became a management concern, and it applies to all saltwater fishing regardless of species. Anyone born in or after 1980 who operates a vessel of eight to fifteen metres or an engine producing more than 25 horsepower must hold a boating certificate, which is a safety qualification rather than a fishing licence and is obtained through a one-day course. The requirement is specific to the vessel and engine size, not to the fishing itself, and anglers fishing from smaller boats or from the shore are not affected.

sections.heading: The export cap and the registered camp
sections.body: Norway limits how much fish a visiting angler may take out of the country, and the limit is not generous. The standard tourist allowance is fifteen kilograms of fish, which may be exported twice per calendar year, and the fish must have been caught on rod and handline. The cap applies per person, and exceeding it at the border is an offence under Norwegian customs regulations. There is a larger allowance available, but only for anglers who fish through a registered tourist fishing business — a camp or operator that reports its anglers' catches to the Directorate of Fisheries. The registered business arrangement exists because the Norwegian government wants catch data from the recreational sector, and the reporting obligation is the price of the larger export allowance. The limits are periodically revised, and the Directorate has reduced them in recent years in response to stock assessments, so the figure to check before travelling is the one currently published on fiskeridir.no rather than the one a guidebook printed last winter. The export rules do not apply to fish consumed in Norway — they govern what crosses the border on the way home. Within Norway, there is no limit on how much you keep for personal consumption, though the Directorate advises anglers to take only what they will eat.

sections.heading: Skrei season is a winter fishery
sections.body: The skrei — the migratory Arctic cod that gives the Lofoten fishery its name — arrive off the islands from January through April, driven by the spawning instinct rather than water temperature in the way that temperate species migrate. The fish have spent several years feeding in the Barents Sea and return to the Lofoten wall to spawn in the cold, clear water along the archipelago's western edge. The fishery has sustained coastal communities for a thousand years, and the modern recreational version of it — jigging for skrei from small boats off the islands — is a winter pursuit that requires cold-weather gear as much as fishing tackle. The banks off Vestfjorden, between the Lofoten wall and the mainland, are the primary ground, and the depth at which skrei hold varies with the tide and the light: slack tide and overcast conditions tend to bring the fish higher in the water column, which is when the jigging is most productive. The skrei are not the only species available — Atlantic halibut, coalfish and large ling are all present on the same banks — but the skrei migration is the event that defines the season, and the charter operators in the Lofoten build their winter programmes around it. The midnight sun season, from late May through July, is a different fishery entirely, targeting the resident species when the islands are accessible and the weather is milder.

sections.heading: Free to fish, constrained by closure
sections.body: Fishing with handheld tackle along the Swedish coast, including the Stockholm archipelago, requires no permit and carries no fee. This is not allemansrätten — the right of public access does not itself cover fishing, which is a separate right established by fisheries law rather than the constitutional tradition that governs camping and foraging. The coastal fishing freedom is specific to saltwater and specific to rod and handline; it does not extend to inland waters within the archipelago, where the water owner's permission is still required, and it does not override the closed areas that are the real constraint on pike fishing here. Länsstyrelsen Stockholm, the county administrative board, has designated sixty-two bays in the archipelago where fishing is banned during the spring spawning period, and nine of those bays are closed to fishing year-round. In addition, fourteen protected areas at river mouths are closed in autumn while sea trout run upstream. The closures are not theoretical — they cover many of the shallow, weedy bays that pike prefer for spawning, and the county has registered some three hundred pike spawning sites in the archipelago. The board publishes the protected areas as a downloadable PDF and maintains the rules at svenskafiskeregler.lansstyrelsen.se, and states explicitly that the angler is responsible for knowing which rules apply before casting. The closure map is the first thing to check, not the last.

sections.heading: The mercury advisory
sections.body: Livsmedelsverket, the Swedish National Food Agency, lists pike among the freshwater species that can carry elevated mercury levels, and the advice is specific: anyone who is pregnant, breastfeeding or trying to conceive should eat pike no more than two to three times per year. The same advice covers perch, zander and burbot from the same waters, because mercury accumulates in predatory freshwater fish regardless of which species sits at the top of the local food chain. The mechanism is well understood: mercury enters the water system from natural geological sources and from atmospheric deposition, and it concentrates up the food chain, so larger, older pike from slower, more humic waters carry the highest levels. The advice varies between waters — some archipelago bays have locally measured figures that are lower than others — and the county board and municipality hold the local data. The advisory is not a reason to stop fishing the archipelago; catch-and-release is entirely unaffected by it, and the pike fishery here is predominantly release-oriented for the larger spawning fish anyway. It is a reason to know what you are keeping and to check the local figures before you make a meal of a catch. The advisory is published on Livsmedelsverket's website and is separate from the fishing regulations, which govern whether you may fish, not whether you should eat what you catch.

sections.heading: Spring is the season, and the season is short
sections.body: The archipelago pike fishery peaks in spring, from April through May, when the pike move into the shallow bays to spawn and are aggressively feeding before and after the event. The water is cold, the bays are shallow enough to warm in the sun, and the pike are visible and catchable in water that is often waist-deep from the shore. The spring window is the reason the county board closes sixty-two bays during this period — the fishing pressure on spawning pike would be unsustainable without the closures, and the closure list is effectively a map of where the best fishing would be if it were permitted. Outside the spring window, the pike disperse into deeper water and the archipelago fishery shifts to the autumn, from September through November, when the fish are feeding heavily before winter and the water has cooled enough to oxygenate well. Winter fishing is possible but weather-dependent, and the archipelago is exposed to Baltic storms that make small-boat fishing dangerous in anything but calm conditions. The pike here are the same species as across the Baltic, but the brackish water produces slower growth and the fish are typically smaller than their counterparts in the Bothnian Bay or the Finnish archipelago. The sport is in the numbers and the setting rather than the size, and the thirty thousand islands of the archipelago provide a backdrop that no inland fishery matches.

sections.heading: A trout fishery built on top of a hydro reservoir
sections.body: Yingina/Great Lake is a highland plateau lake in Tasmania's Central Highlands, managed by the Inland Fisheries Service as what IFS itself designates a "Premium Wild Trout Fishery," run in partnership with Hydro Tasmania. The lake is a hydroelectric storage rather than a natural fixed-level lake, and its surface can sit many metres below Full Supply Level depending on generation demand. That is why the concrete boat ramps built for full-level conditions can strand a trailer or hide submerged hazards at low water, and why IFS's own guidance is to check the current level before launching rather than trust the ramp being usable. Camping is restricted to the formal ground at Miena, the small township on the lake's shore, rather than informal camping around the rest of the shoreline.

sections.heading: Two threatened natives share the water with the trout
sections.body: Great Lake paragalaxias and Shannon paragalaxias, both listed as threatened, are native to this system alongside the introduced brown and rainbow trout that draw anglers; spotted and climbing galaxias also occur here. IFS's management reflects that dual mandate: brown trout are sustained mainly through natural recruitment rather than heavy stocking, while active enhancement effort is concentrated on the rainbow population, and inlet streams within a set distance of the lake are closed to fishing year-round to protect spawning fish and the native galaxiid populations alike. Using live fish or fish products as bait anywhere on the system is prohibited, which functions as much as a native-species protection measure as a trout-fishery one.

sections.heading: Where the rules tighten: Tods Corner and Canal Bay
sections.body: Most of Yingina/Great Lake is open to fishing year-round, but the Tods Corner and Canal Bay arms run on a defined season instead and are restricted to artificial lures and flies only, with no bait permitted — a stricter rule than the rest of the lake. Bag and minimum-size limits apply lake-wide and differ between brown and rainbow trout, with an additional cap on how many rainbow trout may be retained. Both the season dates and the exact limits are revised between seasons, so confirm the current figures directly with IFS rather than from a number repeated here or elsewhere.

great-lake-tasmania-trout.sourceNotes: Fetched and read directly 23 Sep 2026. Season dates (currently 28 Nov 2026 - 28 Mar 2027 for Tods Corner/Canal Bay), the bag limit (12 fish lake-wide) and the size figures (300mm minimum brown trout; 400mm minimum and a 3-fish cap on rainbow trout) are all on the source page but deliberately not printed per content rule 3 — they are exactly the kind of regulatory figure that is revised between seasons. The prose states that limits exist and differ by species/zone rather than quoting them. Threatened-species and stocking detail (natural recruitment for browns, enhancement focus for rainbows, most recent stocking record a single adult brown in July 2026) is from the same page. No second source was used for this entry — everything here traces to this one IFS page, which is why it is marked full rather than partial despite being a single source.

sections.heading: One park, three separate permits
sections.body: Montauk Point State Park runs its own permit system for fishing rather than folding it into a general park entry fee. The park sells annual sport fishing permits covering most of the year plus a separate short-term permit for the summer window when the annual permit is not on sale, and fishing at the adjoining Camp Hero State Park after dark needs its own distinct night-fishing permit on top of whichever daytime permit is held. Driving a vehicle onto the beach itself is a third, separate authorization again — a 4-wheel-drive beach permit, distinct from both fishing permits and from the day-use vehicle entrance fee. Three different things are being authorized here, not one, and New York State Parks recommends confirming current terms with the park office before a trip rather than assuming last year's rules still apply.

sections.heading: New York doesn't licence saltwater anglers — it registers them
sections.body: New York does not operate a traditional fishing licence for recreational saltwater fishing. Instead, NYSDEC requires anyone aged 16 or older fishing for migratory or marine species in the state's Marine and Coastal District — which includes Montauk — to enrol in the Recreational Marine Fishing Registry, a free, no-fee enrolment (aside from a small optional print/mailing charge) that is valid for one full year from the date of registration, with no lifetime option. This registry is a state requirement layered underneath the park's own fishing permit, not a substitute for it — an angler at Montauk needs both the park permit to fish inside the park boundary and the state registry enrolment to be fishing for a marine species at all.

sections.heading: Striped bass specifically: a slot, not just a minimum
sections.body: NYSDEC manages striped bass under a slot-limit system rather than a single size floor — a fish must fall inside a specific size window to be legally kept, not merely clear one threshold, and the window itself differs between the Hudson River and the marine district that includes Montauk. A strict per-trip retention cap applies on top of the slot, and the open season runs on a defined annual window that is a few weeks longer in marine waters than on the Hudson. Anyone fishing bait for striped bass is required to use a non-offset (inline) circle hook, a gear rule that does not apply when fishing artificial lures. The current slot dimensions, the possession number and the exact season dates are set by NYSDEC (coordinated with the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission's coastwide management plan) and are revised by addendum, so check them directly rather than from a fixed figure repeated here.

sections.heading: No licence, but no free access either
sections.body: Scotland has no general rod licence for salmon fishing, and on the Tay that does not mean open access — it means access runs through private riparian rights instead, let out beat by beat via estates and angling associations. For the stretches nearest Dunkeld, the Dunkeld & Birnam Angling Association sells day and week permits, with concessions for juniors and seniors, covering its own beats on the Tay itself (the Dunkeld beat, the Murthly & Glendelvine beat, and the Stanley/Upper Scone beat) plus a beat on the River Braan and two lochs, booked through its own online system. DBAA's permits cover only its own water, not the river as a whole — other stretches of the Tay are let through entirely different estates or associations, so confirming which body actually holds the beat in question matters before travelling, not after.

sections.heading: A statutory board older than most of the buildings on its banks
sections.body: Above the individual beats sits the Tay District Salmon Fisheries Board, the statutory body empowered to protect and improve fisheries across the whole Tay district, which describes itself as operating since 1863 — among the oldest such boards in Scotland. It is governed by a mix of upper- and lower-proprietor representatives plus co-opted members representing anglers and netsmen, runs its own hatchery near Perth, and employs fisheries officers and biologists managing several thousand miles of river, burn and loch across the catchment. That is the same two-layer structure already documented for the Spey: the beat sells the day, the statutory board sets the conservation rules that apply regardless of which beat you are standing on.

sections.heading: Release rules stronger than the law requires
sections.body: Scottish Government regulation, introduced in January 2015, makes catch-and-release compulsory on the Tay for a defined early-season window running from mid-January to the end of March — every salmon taken in that period must be returned, even a fish that has died. The Board's own guidance goes further: it recommends releasing all salmon and grilse for the rest of the season too, a voluntary extension adopted because spring-run numbers, and since 2016 the summer and autumn grilse runs as well, have kept declining, with exploitation rates on some rivers reported as high as 40 per cent. The mandatory window is a legal floor, not the Board's actual expectation of anglers on the river.

sections.heading: Public access here means a mapped site, not a riverside right
sections.body: Unlike the Tay or the Spey, the Madison in Montana runs through a formal Fishing Access Site (FAS) network operated by Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks — publicly owned parcels along the river rather than a general right to walk the bank. The Ennis FAS, just outside the town of Ennis, is a documented example: a roughly 49-acre site with a gravel boat ramp, on-site camping capped at a short per-stay limit, day-use-only enforced over winter, a trailer-length ceiling, and camping fees that are lower for anglers holding a valid fishing licence than for those without one. Facilities and exact limits vary site to site along the river, so an angler should confirm the specific FAS being used rather than assume every access point on the Madison behaves like Ennis.

sections.heading: Afternoons close first when the river runs hot
sections.body: In drought years the Madison is one of the rivers Montana FWP restricts under what it calls a "hoot owl" rule: fishing is prohibited every day between early afternoon and midnight, rather than the river being closed outright, which lets angling continue during the cooler morning hours when a stressed, warm-water fishery is least able to tolerate the added stress of being caught and released. FWP has applied this to sections of the Madison in past drought summers, sometimes alongside a full round-the-clock closure on a specific stretch when reservoir outflows keep the water too warm even overnight. Because the trigger is water temperature and flow rather than the calendar, whether a hoot-owl restriction is active on any given date has to be checked against FWP's current closures list rather than assumed from the season.
